quick: Osteoarthritis 12.5-25 mg once daily; acute pain 50 mg once daily (short term)
Blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, renal function
summary: Rofecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor NSAID that was used for osteoarthritis, acute pain, and dysmenorrhoea. It was voluntarily withdrawn worldwide in 2004 after trials showed an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke with prolonged use. It is not FDA-approved (withdrawn). Any record reflects historical labelling; it should not be prescribed where withdrawn.

dosage.d: 12.5 mg once daily; may increase to 25 mg once daily

dosage.n: Use of 50 mg/day for more than 5 days was not recommended

admin: Take once daily with or without food
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Swallow tablets whole; oral suspension may be used where available
Note: product was withdrawn from the market for cardiovascular safety reasons
moa: Rofecoxib selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), the inducible enzyme responsible for prostaglandin synthesis at sites of inflammation, reducing prostaglandin-mediated pain and inflammation while largely sparing COX-1 (and thus gastric mucosal prostaglandins). Reduced prostacyclin without comparable reduction in platelet thromboxane is thought to contribute to its prothrombotic cardiovascular risk.

absolute: Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions
Active peptic ulceration or gastrointestinal bleeding
Established ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, or peripheral arterial disease
relative: Cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, smoking)

preg: Avoid in pregnancy. As an NSAID/COX-2 inhibitor, use in the third trimester can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and impaired fetal renal function; avoid throughout unless clearly essential.
lact: Rofecoxib is excreted in milk in animal studies; breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: Avoid in significant renal impairment; COX-2 inhibition reduces renal prostaglandins and can cause fluid retention, oedema, and worsening renal function, particularly in dehydrated or at-risk patients.
hepatic: Avoid in moderate to severe hepatic impairment; use with caution and at low dose in mild impairment with monitoring.

major: Aspirin / other NSAIDs (additive GI toxicity, reduced renal protection)
moderate: ACE inhibitors / ARBs and diuretics (reduced antihypertensive effect, renal impairment)
minor: Rifampicin (reduces rofecoxib levels via metabolism induction)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor blood pressure, renal function, and INR with warfarin

rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

counsel: This medicine was withdrawn worldwide because of an increased risk of heart attack and stroke
Seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, weakness/numbness, or speech difficulty
Report black or bloody stools, severe stomach pain, or vomiting blood
Avoid alcohol; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
Tell your doctor about heart, kidney, liver, or stomach problems
pk: Store at 15-30 C; protect from moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; pending clinical review. (Voluntarily withdrawn worldwide in 2004.)
Withdrawn after the APPROVe trial showed increased myocardial infarction and stroke with prolonged use
Selective COX-2 inhibition spares gastric COX-1 but confers a prothrombotic cardiovascular risk
Avoid in established cardiovascular disease and use the lowest dose for the shortest duration if ever used
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, hypertension, fluid retention, and acute renal failure. Management is supportive with gastric decontamination if early, monitoring of blood pressure and renal function, and treatment of GI bleeding; the drug is highly protein bound so dialysis is unlikely to help. No specific antidote.
